title: Strings
description: Character arrays, the null terminator, string literals, and the core string.h functions.
objectives: Understand that C strings are just char arrays ending in a null terminator
Use strlen, strcpy, strncpy, strcat, strcmp, strchr, and strstr

content.heading: Character Arrays and the Null Terminator
content.body: C has no dedicated string type — a 'string' is just a char array whose logical end is marked by a null byte, '\0' (value 0), rather than being tracked by a separate length field. A string literal like "Hello" is automatically stored with a trailing '\0', so char greeting[] = "Hello"; actually allocates 6 bytes (5 characters plus the terminator), not 5. Every function that operates on 'strings' (printf's %s, strlen, strcpy, and so on) works by scanning forward from a starting address until it finds that '\0' byte — if a char array is missing its terminator (or it was overwritten), these functions will keep reading past the intended end of the buffer, into whatever memory follows, which is undefined behavior.

content.heading: Core string.h Functions
content.body: strlen(s) returns the number of characters before the null terminator (not counting the terminator itself). strcpy(dest, src) copies src into dest, including its terminator — dest must already have enough allocated space, since strcpy performs no bounds checking, one of C's most common sources of buffer overflows; strncpy(dest, src, n) copies at most n characters, safer but with its own subtlety (it does not guarantee dest is null-terminated if src is n characters or longer, so callers often must terminate it manually). strcat(dest, src) appends src onto the end of dest (again, no bounds checking — dest must have room). strcmp(s1, s2) returns 0 if the strings are equal in content, and a positive or negative value reflecting their lexicographic ordering otherwise — never a simple boolean. strchr(s, c) finds the first occurrence of character c; strstr(haystack, needle) finds the first occurrence of substring needle.

content.explanation: greeting[20] leaves enough room for strcat's appended text plus the terminator. strcmp returning 0 (not a truthy 1) for equal strings is a very common point of confusion coming from other languages.

keyPoints: A C string is a char array ending in a '\0' byte, not a distinct type with its own length
strcpy()/strcat() perform no bounds checking — the destination buffer must already be large enough
strcmp() returns 0 for equal strings, not a truthy value — always compare its result to 0 explicitly
Every string buffer must have room for its content plus one extra byte for the terminator
commonMistakes: Sizing a char array for exactly the visible characters, forgetting the extra byte for the null terminator
Using strcpy/strcat on a buffer too small for the result, causing a buffer overflow
Treating strcmp()'s return value as a boolean instead of comparing it to 0
